canonical_facts: Dunmarrow's gate closes in roughly forty minutes.
Four bodies hang from the execution tree outside town.
One body moved.
Two gate guards have seen the player approaching but appear not to have noticed the movement.
Fresh muddy footprints lead from Dunmarrow to the tree and do not return.
A small geometric transfer symbol is cut into the bark beneath the fourth body.
The Black Tithe remains a working central mystery, not a predetermined single explanation.
The player used Resonance Sense on the hidden disturbance in the drainage ditch.
The sensed effect appears to be actively redirecting motion through the ditch water rather than simply moving the water directly.
The tree carving and the ditch disturbance appear to participate in the same transfer geometry, but the exact relationship is not yet understood.
The player directly asked the concealed ditch entity whether it was their enemy.
The player shouted to alert the Dunmarrow gate guards while keeping the concealed ditch entity in view.
The concealed entity had previously said it was not the player's enemy unless made into one and demanded that the hanging man be cut down.
The player rushed to the execution tree and cut through the active transfer carving with the long knife.
A strong technical read let the player sever the geometry cleanly rather than merely damaging the bark.
The transfer structure collapsed immediately.
The abnormal motion in the ditch ceased.
The hanging man's movements stopped feeding the ditch effect.
The concealed entity lost part of whatever effect had hidden or sustained it.
The player chose to help the hanging man rather than pursue the fleeing entity.
The player cut the hanging man down without causing a serious fall.
The hanging man was alive but weak, with obvious neck compression and breathing difficulty.
The player immediately explained the active transfer mark, the hidden ditch figure, and the abnormal water movement to the approaching guard.
The concealed figure escaped farther along the drainage ditch while attention shifted to the victim.
The player chose not to pursue the escaped entity or investigate the missing boot.
The player left Edrin Vale and the execution-site evidence in the guards' custody.
Dunmarrow closes its town gates at dusk, but there is no established general stay-indoors curfew.
The player chose to meet Dunmarrow's reeve immediately after entering town.
The meeting takes place in the gatehouse while Edrin Vale is being treated nearby.

The player gave Reeve Maelin Voss a complete truthful account of the execution-ground incident, including speaking to the concealed entity, using Resonance Sense, the entity's demand to cut Edrin down, the transfer link, alerting the guards, severing the mark, seeing the fleeing figure, and Edrin's missing boot.
The player reconstructed the execution-tree transfer mark from memory for Reeve Maelin Voss.
The reconstruction preserved the two-receiver structure and the severed hooked diagonal closely enough to support further analysis.
After the dormant bell tower rang and Resonance Sense reacted, the player asked Reeve Maelin Voss whether she wanted to investigate it.
The player urged the group to hurry to the old bell tower.
The player, Reeve Maelin Voss, and two watchmen reached the tower without stopping to investigate anything else en route.
The player ordered the group to stay together: investigate below the bell tower first, then go upstairs.
The player explicitly checked whether anyone in the group had a shield before committing.
The player attempted to sever the active transfer path beneath the bell tower using the same principle as at the execution tree.
The older network contained redundant/overflow routing. The cut did not stop the system; it caused a violent local discharge through the player's knife and arm.
The player took 4 damage, dropped the knife, and suffered temporary numbness/shock in the weapon hand.
The discharge fed additional motion into the bell above, causing it to ring again.
The failure revealed that this network reroutes interrupted transfer rather than simply collapsing when one path is cut.
After the failed cut, the player recovered the knife with the left hand and paused to observe the underground bell-tower transfer network before going upstairs.
A strong observation showed the basin objects act as person-specific anchors, while the iron rods carry transferred mechanical energy upward.
The network has redundant channels, but the rerouting is not instantaneous: there are brief moments where pressure shifts between paths.
The bell above is acting as a major receiver/reservoir and is currently closer to another discharge than before.
The player identified that blindly cutting more channels is likely to worsen the situation.
The player ordered a shield-and-reach formation on the spiral stair.
Harl holds the choke point with shield raised while Joren uses the spear from behind him; the player remains behind them due to the impaired right hand.
During the stairwell fight, the player used Vector Knot against the robed man's committed downhill lunge.
The player redirected a small portion of the attacker's existing momentum sideways and downward into the inner stair geometry rather than trying to stop him outright.
The attacker lost his footing, struck the stone steps/inner wall, and collapsed immediately in front of Harl's shield.
The shield-and-spear formation prevented the falling attacker from crashing through into the player.
The player attacked the prone robed man with the long knife using the left hand while the right remained impaired.
The attack landed cleanly and caused a serious but not immediately fatal wound.
The player ordered the group to hold formation and stop attacking the bell-linked man.
The player explicitly recognized two constraints: blindly damaging the underground network is dangerous, and injuring the linked man feeds the bell.
The player used Resonance Sense at point-blank range on the bell-linked man's throat markings while the party held formation and stopped attacking.
The throat markings are not themselves the full transfer circuit; they are a keyed coupling layer that ties the man's pulse and involuntary movement to the tower network.
The connection has a narrow synchronization point just below the left side of the jaw where three carved lines converge.
The bell is receiving the man's movement and physiological shock as transferable mechanical input.
The connection can likely be interrupted by breaking synchronization rather than by cutting flesh or destroying the main network.
A brief disruption of rhythm, pressure, or alignment at the convergence point may be enough to desynchronize the coupling.
Because the link is keyed to the man, a prepared Waymark could potentially be used as a temporary false receiver if the timing is precise.
The player prepared a Waymark on the inner stair wall as a false receiver for the bell-linked man's keyed transfer.
The player tuned the Waymark to imitate the man's coupling signature closely enough for the network to recognize it during a reroute window.
At the moment the network shifted paths, the player used Vector Knot to redirect the live transfer into the prepared Waymark.
The false receiver accepted the transfer long enough to desynchronize the man from the bell without further injuring him.
The Waymark overloaded and fractured after the transfer, but the discharge went into the stone wall rather than into a person.
The bell's motion dropped sharply once the living link was broken.
One bronze waymark nail was consumed/damaged in the overloaded false receiver.
The player attempted to recover Resonance by attuning a fresh Wayfarer working to the bell network rather than siphoning stored mechanical energy directly.
The attunement failed: the ancient network did not accept the player's pattern as a stable participant.
No Resonance was recovered and no additional damage was taken.
The failed attunement produced a return pulse that made it clear the newly opened structure below is now the strongest active node in the local transfer network.
The party returned downstairs without splitting.
The newly opened mechanism revealed a lower passage beneath the original basement chamber.
The player remained at 6/10 HP, 0/3 Resonance, with the right hand still impaired.
At the lower well chamber, the player refused to return anything blindly and demanded that the unseen speaker identify itself first.
The player asked the entity known as Keeper Below to explain its role.
The player challenged the Keeper Below to provide evidence that its explanation was truthful.
The player accepted the Keeper Below's reversible test.
The party stayed together, retrieved Edrin Vale's missing boot from the basin above, and returned to the lower well chamber.
The player kept physical possession of the boot and did not place it into the socket or surrender it.
When the boot was brought close to Edrin Vale's carved name, the name and empty socket reacted immediately.
The boot pulled slightly toward the socket as if under tension, while the chain below slackened a fraction.
The bell above did not ring.
The reaction occurred before the boot touched the socket, supporting the Keeper's claim that the personal object functions as a keyed token tied to Edrin's claim.
The player inserted Edrin Vale's missing boot into the keyed socket beside his name while the party held formation.
The socket accepted the token without violent discharge.
Edrin Vale's carved name faded from active resonance and the chain below slackened significantly.
The bell remained still.
The boot lost its keyed resonance and became an ordinary damaged personal object after the claim released.
The result strongly supports the Keeper Below's claim that placing the keyed token releases the stored claim associated with that person.
After releasing Edrin Vale's claim, the player asked the Keeper Below for a physical item in exchange for continued help.
The player accepted the Keeper Below's Ledger Shard reward.
The Ledger Shard is now in the player's possession.
The shard gives a slight physical pull when brought near an object participating in a genuine magical claim, keyed link, prepared transfer, or bound relationship.
The shard does not identify purpose, danger, creator, or target; it only confirms that a real connection exists.
GM correction: the player has not agreed to release additional claims, revive anyone, or work for the Keeper Below. Any such future involvement requires an explicit player choice.
The player ended involvement in the bell-tower investigation for the night and told Reeve Maelin Voss to come find them if further help was needed.
Reeve Maelin Voss accepted the boundary and did not pressure the player to continue immediately.
No new plot event was introduced solely to prevent the player from leaving.
The player paid 2 silver for supper and a bed at a travelers' inn.
A safe full night's rest restored 4 HP under the locked recovery formula: floor(25% of 10 max HP) + CON modifier 2.
The player's temporary right-hand shock/numbness cleared because it had not been recorded as a true Wound.
Resonance remained at 0/3 because sleep does not automatically restore Resonance.
No one came to fetch the player during the night.
The player returned to the old bell tower the next morning specifically to visit the Keeper Below.
The player was allowed back into the secured tower because of their direct involvement in the previous night's investigation.
The player descended to the lower well chamber without restarting the broader investigation.
The player told the Keeper Below: 'You are very powerful.'
The Keeper Below described its power as narrow, old, and domain-bound rather than general omnipotence.
The player asked the Keeper Below whether it had once been human.
The Keeper Below answered that it had once been human, but implied that the transformation into its present role was gradual and bound to the system it serves.
The player asked the Keeper Below whether it wanted freedom.
The Keeper Below did not give an immediate simple yes/no answer; it expressed uncertainty about what freedom would mean after so long bound to its role.
The player asked the Keeper Below who the most powerful human it had ever met was.
The Keeper named Sereth Vale, a human transfer-worker remembered for extreme precision and control rather than spectacle.

According to the Keeper, Sereth could redirect structural loads, momentum, heat, and pressure across prepared systems without collapsing them, and once stabilized a failing stone bridge long enough for hundreds to cross.
The Keeper described Sereth as powerful because she understood limits well enough to act at the edge of them without losing control.
The player asked the Keeper Below to teach them.
The Keeper Below agreed in principle to teach within its domains: claims, bindings, keyed transfers, anchors, conservation, and precise transfer structure.
The Keeper made clear that instruction would not instantly grant mastery; learning would require demonstration, practice, correction, and risk-appropriate exercises.
During the first formal lesson, the player defined transfer as 'magic from one point to another.'

The Keeper corrected the definition: transfer magic does not simply move 'magic'; it establishes a lawful relationship in which a specific quantity, state, or claim moves or is reassigned from a source to a receiver under defined constraints.
The Keeper emphasized that source, transferable quantity, receiver, compatibility, capacity, and consequence must all be identified.
In the Keeper's first transfer lesson, the player correctly answered that transferring momentum out of the larger moving weight should reduce the larger weight's momentum.
During a supervised Keeper lesson, the player attempted to transfer a small portion of a swinging iron weight's sideways momentum into a smaller hanging weight.
The control attempt critically failed: the player coupled too early and at a poor angle, causing the smaller weight to twist rather than swing cleanly.
The Keeper terminated the supplied transfer structure before the chains or player were harmed.
No Resonance was spent because the Keeper supplied the active magical structure.
The failure was informative and directly demonstrated that timing and receiver alignment matter separately from choosing a small transfer amount.
On the second supervised momentum-transfer attempt, the player delayed the coupling until the smaller receiver aligned with its natural swing path and used a conservative transfer amount.
The player succeeded cleanly: the larger weight lost a small amount of sideways momentum and the smaller weight gained a controlled swing with minimal twist.
The Keeper's supplied structure remained stable and no Resonance was spent.
The player attempted their first supervised momentum-capture exercise using the Keeper's iron retention ring.
The player successfully captured a very small amount of momentum from the larger swinging weight and held it briefly, but retention decayed noticeably before release.
The release into the smaller weight worked, though weaker than the original captured amount and with a slight delay.
No Resonance was spent because the Keeper supplied the active structure.
The exercise demonstrated that capture, retention, decay, and release are distinct skills.
The player continued supervised momentum capture practice for roughly forty minutes.
The Keeper varied source speed, receiver angle, and retention duration to prevent rote repetition.
Across several attempts, the player learned to notice retention decay before the iron ring's vibration made it obvious.
The player can now perform a tiny supervised capture-hold-release sequence with some consistency, but cannot yet use it independently in combat.
The player attempted their first self-built momentum capture relationship using the Keeper's iron retention ring as the storage medium.

The player succeeded strongly: they identified the moving weight as source, opened a compatible coupling to the ring, captured a small amount of sideways momentum, held it briefly through visible decay, and released it cleanly into the smaller receiver.
The Keeper did not construct the capture relationship for this attempt.
The retention ring still acted as an external storage aid, so the player has not yet learned free capture without a prepared medium.
No Resonance was spent because the exercise drew on the Keeper's training apparatus rather than the player's personal reserve.
The player proposed using their own body as the retention medium for captured momentum.

The Keeper confirmed that a living body can participate as a receiver/storage medium, but warned that retained momentum must exist as real stresses, motion tendencies, deformation, or other physical state rather than disappearing abstractly.
Under supervision, the player attempted a very small body-retention capture.
The attempt failed: the player coupled the stored momentum too locally into the right arm/shoulder instead of distributing it through a stable whole-body structure.
The Keeper terminated the training structure before serious injury occurred.
The player lost 1 HP from strain and gained a temporary right shoulder/wrist strain, but suffered no persistent Wound.
No Resonance was spent because the Keeper supplied the training apparatus.
The player immediately retried body-retention while still strained.
Because the right shoulder/wrist strain was active, the retry was resolved with disadvantage.
The player consciously distributed the captured load through feet, legs, hips, and torso rather than localizing it in the arm.
The attempt partially succeeded: a very small amount of momentum was retained across the player's stance for less than a second and then released safely into the ground through a controlled step.
The strain did not worsen and no additional HP was lost.
The player still cannot reliably retain momentum in the body under combat pressure.
The Keeper advanced body-retention training from simple safe release into the ground to deliberate release into controlled movement.
Because the player was still carrying a temporary right shoulder/wrist strain, the attempt was made under disadvantage.
The player captured a very small amount of momentum, distributed it successfully through feet, legs, hips, and torso, held it briefly, then released it into a forward step.
The movement was noticeably stronger than an ordinary step but remained controlled and did not aggravate the existing strain.
This was the player's first successful body-retention-to-movement sequence.

The Keeper advanced the lesson to weapon-mediated release: capture a tiny amount of momentum, retain it through the whole body, and release it through the walking staff into a separate hanging target.
The exercise was chosen to test whether the player could route stored momentum through stance, hands, and weapon without localizing dangerous load in the already strained right shoulder/wrist.

The player succeeded partially: the retained momentum transferred through the staff and moved the target, but some of the load bled into the hands and shoulders, making the strike less efficient than intended.
The existing strain did not worsen and no additional HP was lost.
The player learned that a weapon becomes part of the transfer structure and must be aligned, braced, and compatible with the release vector.
The Keeper advanced the lesson to delayed weapon release against a moving receiver.
The player had to capture momentum from one pendulum, retain it through the whole body, wait for a second pendulum to align, and then release through the walking staff.
The active shoulder/wrist strain continued to impose disadvantage.

The player succeeded cleanly: they captured conservatively, held through brief decay, waited for alignment, and released through the staff into the moving target without losing balance or worsening the strain.
The exercise demonstrated that retention can create tactical timing windows rather than merely increasing force.
The Keeper advanced training to unpredictable incoming motion using several possible release channels.
The player had to read the source in real time, decide whether to capture, and route any retained momentum through the whole body.
Because the existing shoulder/wrist strain remained active, the attempt was made under disadvantage.
SYSTEM provenance: the disadvantage rolls were 12 and natural 1, so the natural 1 governed the result.
The player misread the incoming line, coupled too late, and localized part of the retained load into the already strained right side.
The Keeper terminated the supplied structure before a severe injury occurred, but the player took 2 HP of strain and the temporary shoulder/wrist condition worsened.
No Resonance was spent.
The player stopped body-retention training after the aggravated shoulder/wrist strain rather than risking a persistent Wound.
The player returned to the travelers' inn and paid the previously established 2 silver for food and a safe bed.
The player spent the remainder of the day resting and completed a safe full night's rest.
Safe full rest restored 4 HP under the locked recovery formula, capped at maximum HP: 7/10 -> 10/10.
The aggravated shoulder/wrist strain cleared because it remained a temporary condition and had not become a persistent Wound.
Resonance remained at 0/3 because sleep does not automatically restore Resonance.
No new event was introduced solely to interrupt the player's rest.
The player returned to the Keeper Below after fully recovering from the previous training strain.
The Keeper resumed instruction with reactive retention drills, now without injury disadvantage.
The lesson goal remained decision quality as much as execution: identify which incoming motions are safe to capture and which should be allowed to pass.
In the Keeper's reactive retention drill, the player chose the second incoming slider: lighter and faster, arriving diagonally downward from the left.
The choice traded easier total load for more difficult alignment and required body rotation during reception.
SYSTEM provenance: the reactive retention roll was 18.
The player succeeded strongly by rotating through the hips and stance, taking only a small portion of the slider's momentum and avoiding localization in the shoulder.
The captured momentum was retained briefly and released safely into a controlled step rather than dumped through the arms.
The Keeper judged the choice as valid rather than optimal by default: the player demonstrated that capacity and geometry must be weighed together.
In the Keeper's reactive retention drill, the player refused the third slider because its rattling track and wobbling motion made the incoming vector unreliable.
The Keeper confirmed that refusing the third slider was sound judgment: uncertainty in direction can make a modest load more dangerous than a heavier but predictable one.
The Keeper removed the fixed tracks and advanced training to free-moving incoming motion.
A small weighted training mass was released on a loose suspension, allowing drift and rotation rather than guaranteeing a fixed vector.
SYSTEM provenance: the player's reactive retention roll was 15.
The player delayed commitment until the mass's actual line became readable, then captured only a small stable component of its motion.
The player retained that motion briefly through whole-body structure and released it into a controlled lateral step.

The attempt succeeded without injury and demonstrated that the player can read and selectively capture part of a free-moving vector rather than treating the entire object's motion as one indivisible quantity.
The Keeper advanced retention training to controlled physical impact using a leather-wrapped free-swinging training weight aimed at the player's torso.
The player was instructed not to stop the entire strike, but to capture only a readable portion at contact while allowing the remaining force to pass through ordinary body movement.
SYSTEM provenance: the reactive contact-retention roll was 13.

The player succeeded: they accepted the ordinary impact with a small backward give, captured a limited component of the incoming momentum through the torso and stance, held it briefly, and released it into the recovery step.
The attempt caused no HP loss and no Wound.
The Keeper's apparatus still supplied the active magical scaffold; the player spent no Resonance.

The Keeper advanced impact-retention training into a chained transfer: receive a controlled torso strike, retain only a safe fraction, preserve footing, then release the retained momentum through the walking staff into a separate target before decay.
SYSTEM provenance: the chained impact-retention roll was 12.

The player partially succeeded: they captured a safe fraction of the impact and kept their footing, then transferred it through the staff into the target, but noticeable retention decay and grip losses reduced the final effect.
The player suffered no injury and spent no Resonance because the Keeper's apparatus still supplied the active magical scaffold.
This exercise confirmed that chained transfers compound losses across capture, retention, body routing, weapon coupling, and final release.
The Keeper repeated the chained impact-retention drill at the same force, focusing only on efficiency.
SYSTEM provenance: the efficiency drill roll was 17.

The player captured a conservative portion of the torso impact, minimized retention delay, aligned the body and grip with the staff, and released into the separate target with substantially reduced losses.
The target received a clearly stronger transfer than in the previous attempt while the player maintained balance and suffered no injury.
This was the player's first clean, repeatable completion of the full chain: impact -> selective capture -> body retention -> staff coupling -> separate receiver.
The Keeper removed its active magical scaffold from the transfer exercise while leaving the prepared retention ring, weights, and staff in place.
The player had to construct the capture relationship personally rather than merely operating inside a relationship sustained by the Keeper.
SYSTEM provenance: the self-constructed transfer roll was 16.
The player successfully established source -> prepared retention ring -> body/weapon routing without the Keeper holding the path open.
The prepared retention ring itself remained an attuned magical medium, so the exercise did not consume the player's personal Resonance.
This was the player's first successful full transfer structure built and operated without the Keeper actively sustaining the coupling.
The player is not yet field-independent because the prepared ring is still doing important structural work.
The Keeper removed the prepared retention ring from the exercise.
To avoid contradicting the player's empty Resonance reserve, the Keeper continued supplying the magical power source but did not provide the capture relationship or storage structure.
The player had to use their own body as the retention medium and construct the full source-to-body relationship personally.
SYSTEM provenance: the no-ring body-retention roll was 14.

The player succeeded: they captured a very small amount of momentum, distributed it through feet, legs, hips, and torso, held it briefly, and released it into a controlled step without localizing the load into a joint.
No Resonance was spent because the Keeper supplied the external power; the player is still not field-independent.
Because the player's Resonance reserve was empty, the Keeper did not allow an impossible self-powered retention attempt.
The Keeper instead taught a supervised Resonance attunement exercise using the training pendulum and the compatible old transfer stonework as the external causal source.
The player did not store the pendulum's bulk momentum. Repeated controlled coupling was used to establish a bounded personal magical reserve from the compatible apparatus/site.
SYSTEM provenance: the Resonance attunement roll was 14.
The player successfully established 1 point of personal Resonance.
This method currently depends on a compatible prepared source/site and Keeper supervision; it is not yet a universal rest-based recovery method.
The player attempted their first fully self-powered body-retention transfer using 1 point of personal Resonance.
No prepared retention ring and no Keeper-supplied power or coupling scaffold were used.
SYSTEM provenance: the self-powered retention roll was 8.
The player successfully established the relationship and began capture, but the coupling degraded under load before stable retention was achieved.
The player safely dumped the captured momentum into the ground through their stance rather than forcing the failing hold.
The attempt caused no HP loss and no Wound.
The committed Resonance was spent: Resonance 1/3 -> 0/3.
The player has demonstrated partial self-powered function but has not yet unlocked a combat-reliable independent retention technique.
The player repeated the supervised Resonance attunement exercise and successfully rebuilt 1 point of Resonance.
SYSTEM provenance: Resonance attunement roll was 15.
The player immediately spent that point on a second fully self-powered body-retention attempt.
SYSTEM provenance: the self-powered retention retry roll was 17.

The player established the source-to-body coupling, captured a small readable component of the moving weight's momentum, distributed it through whole-body structure, held it briefly, and released it safely into a controlled step.
No prepared retention ring, Keeper-supplied power, or Keeper-sustained coupling was used during the retention attempt.
The committed Resonance was spent: 1/3 -> 0/3.
This was the player's first clean successful fully self-powered body-retention transfer under controlled conditions.
The technique is not yet considered combat-reliable because it has not been demonstrated under unpredictable hostile timing.
The player rebuilt personal Resonance before the first hostile-timing retention drill.

SYSTEM provenance: the supervised Resonance attunement roll was a natural 20. The result produced an exceptionally clean 1-point attunement but did not exceed the bounded training method's normal 1-point yield.

The incoming strike arrived on a poor capture line that would have concentrated load through the upper body.

Because no retention was attempted, the player's 1 point of Resonance was preserved.
No HP was lost and no Wound occurred.

The Keeper immediately followed with a second unpredictable padded-staff attack, this time on a cleaner line toward the player's ribs.
The player chose to attempt fully self-powered body retention under hostile timing.

The player recognized the safe capture window, took only a limited component of the strike's momentum, distributed it through whole-body structure, preserved footing, and released it into a short lateral recovery step.
The padded strike still made contact as an ordinary controlled training blow; the magic reduced and redirected part of its momentum rather than erasing the impact.
No HP was lost and no Wound occurred.
The player's 1 point of Resonance was spent: 1/3 -> 0/3.
This was the player's first clean successful fully self-powered body-retention transfer under unpredictable hostile timing.
